title: Dealignment, Not Realignment
hook: Working-class voters have been about a third of the American electorate for seventy years. What changed is not their size but their attachment — they left one party without joining the other.
key_points: Working-class self-identification has held steady near 35% of voters for 70 years, at 38% in 2024.
Democratic support among that group peaked around 56% in 1960 and stands near 30% today.
A majority of working-class voters identified as Democrats in 1958; none has since, and only in 2020–2024 did more identify as Republican than Democrat.
Jacobs's claim: the gap grew mainly because party positions moved, not because working-class views did.
Attitude gaps widened across the board — government waste from 5 points in 1958 to 27 in 2024; equality priorities 28 points by 2024.
On trade, 74% of both groups favored import limits in 1988; by 2024 it was 26% of Democrats against 54% of working-class voters.
content_html: The standard story about working-class voters is a story about switching sides. Nicholas Jacobs, who holds the Goldfarb Family Distinguished Chair in American Government at Colby College, argues in The Conversation that the data support something less tidy: a group detaching from party politics rather than migrating across it.
extra_html:
Start with what has not changed. The share of voters who call themselves working class has hovered around 35% for seventy years and stood at 38% in 2024. What moved is attachment. Democratic support within the group peaked near 56% in 1960 and sits around 30% today; a majority identified as Democrats in 1958 and never has again. Only in the 2020–2024 window did more working-class voters identify as Republican than Democrat — which is why Jacobs calls them "politically homeless" rather than realigned.

His causal claim is that the parties moved. Where Democrats and working-class voters broadly agreed in 1984 that reducing inequality would ease social problems, by 2024 Democrats were 28 points more likely to prioritize equality concerns. The gap on whether government wastes money grew from 5 points in 1958 to 27 in 2024. Approval gaps of 20 to 30 points opened on health care expansion, environmental spending and jobs programs, alongside cultural divides on traditional family values (25 points), religion's importance (17), abortion (30) and immigration levels (24). Trade is the sharpest illustration: 74% of both groups favored import limits in 1988, but by 2024 only 26% of Democrats did, against 54% of working-class voters. Jacobs argues the divergence is about worldview — fairness, personal responsibility, trust in institutions after deindustrialization, trade deals, the 2008 foreclosures and the opioid crisis — which is why he thinks "fight the oligarchy" messaging and blue-collar biography misdiagnose the problem. That conclusion is his interpretation and other analysts read the same trends as ordinary education-based realignment; the durable takeaway is the distinction itself. A party losing a group to the opposition has a persuasion problem. A party losing it to detachment has a much harder one.

related.title: Why Outsiders Keep Capturing 'Establishment' Parties
related.hook: Modern parties look powerful on television and weak up close — most have little real control over who runs under their banner. That gap is what lets outsider candidates walk in and take over.

related.hook: Many voters no longer back a candidate they admire — they vote to keep the other party out. That 'negative partisanship' can make even scandal forgivable.

flashcards.prompt: What is the difference between dealignment and realignment?
flashcards.back_html: Realignment means a group switches parties. Dealignment means it detaches from both — Jacobs describes working-class voters as "politically homeless" rather than captured by the other side.

flashcards.prompt: Jacobs argues the working-class–Democratic gap opened mainly because of what?

choices.text: Democratic positions moving left while working-class views stayed comparatively stable
Working-class voters adopting conservative views on economics
A sharp decline in the share of voters who call themselves working class

flashcards.explanation_html: Self-identification stayed near 35% for decades. Jacobs attributes the divergence to party movement — on equality, trade, government trust and cultural questions — rather than to the group shifting rightward.

flashcards.prompt: Which figure best illustrates the trade divergence Jacobs cites?

choices.text: In 1988, 74% of both groups favored import limits; by 2024, 26% of Democrats did versus 54% of working-class voters
Support for import limits rose in both groups to over 80%
Neither group has ever favored import limits

flashcards.explanation_html: Trade protection was once common ground. The gap that opened by 2024 is one of his clearest examples of positions moving apart.
